subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: spending it all at once on impulse [Pitfall]
passage:
Sunday. Pocket money day! I bought two sticker sheets and a big bag of sweets straight away and passed them along the whole bench. Best day ever.
Friday of the second week. I looked in my tin. Nothing, not one coin. And tomorrow is Gopika's birthday. Amma said a small gift would be nice. All I have is an empty tin and stickers already stuck in my book. My face went hot at school when everyone talked about presents. I will give her a drawing, I guess. I hope she does not mind. - Pranav

qa.q: When did Pranav spend the pocket money?
qa.a: Pranav spent it straight away on pocket money day.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel at school when everyone talked about presents?
qa.a: Embarrassed, since Pranav's face went hot, having nothing left to buy a gift with.

qa.q: What could Pranav do differently next time, and why?
qa.a: Pranav could set aside a small part for surprises like birthdays before buying treats, so the tin is not empty by week two.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel about receiving a drawing?
qa.a: Gopika may be touched that it was made for her, though she might have expected a bought gift.

grounding: A child spends all the pocket money at once on stickers and sweets, and has nothing left for a friend's gift.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: spending it all at once on impulse [Pitfall]
passage: On the first Sunday of the month, Nilesh's Dada pressed forty rupees into his palm at the weekly haat in their village. By sunset Nilesh had spent it all: a sheet of shiny cricket stickers, a stick of orange candy, a paper cone of jaggery peanuts and a spinning top he played with once. He stuck the stickers all over his slate and felt rich. The next Sunday, his friend Deepak mentioned that his birthday was on Wednesday. Everyone was bringing something small: a pencil, an eraser, a keyring. Nilesh turned out his pocket and found a peanut shell and one bent sticker. On Wednesday he stood at the back while the others handed over their gifts, his hands pushed deep in his pockets. Deepak smiled at him anyway, but Nilesh walked home quiet.

qa.q: What did Nilesh buy at the haat?
qa.a: A sheet of shiny cricket stickers, a stick of orange candy, a paper cone of jaggery peanuts and a spinning top.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling as he stood at the back on Wednesday?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and left out, which shows in his hands pushed deep in his pockets while others gave gifts.

qa.q: What other approach might have left Nilesh something for Wednesday?
qa.a: Keeping part of the forty rupees aside for things that come up, or making Deepak a small handmade gift, would have let him join in.

qa.q: How might Deepak have seen Nilesh at the birthday?
qa.a: Deepak smiled at him anyway, so he seemed to care more about Nilesh being there than about a present.

grounding: A child spends all his pocket money on the first day and has nothing left for a friend's birthday gift the next week.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: spending it all at once on impulse [Pitfall]
passage: Every second Friday, Fatima's mother gave her ten dollars. This time Fatima spent all of it before she even reached home in Toronto: a pack of glitter stickers from the corner shop, a sherbet dip, a bag of gummy worms, and a second pack of stickers because the first had no unicorns. By Sunday the gummy worms were gone and the stickers covered her lunchbox. The next Thursday, Soo-ah handed out small paper invitations to a birthday picnic on Saturday. Fatima's stomach dropped. She checked her jacket pockets, her pencil case and under her bed. Twelve cents. She asked her mother for an early allowance, and her mother gently shook her head. On Saturday Fatima gave Soo-ah a folded card with a drawing, and stood quietly while the other presents were opened.

qa.q: How much money did Fatima find when she searched?
What does Fatima's stomach dropping suggest?
qa.a: She felt a jolt of worry and regret on realising she had nothing left for Soo-ah's present. 😔

qa.q: Which approach would have suited Fatima better when the ten dollars arrived?
qa.a: Waiting a day or two before buying anything, or keeping some back, because invitations and other plans often turn up later in the fortnight.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel about the drawn card?
qa.a: Soo-ah may well like a handmade card; it is Fatima who seems uneasy while the other presents are opened.

grounding: A child spends her whole allowance on impulse and has nothing for a friend's birthday the following week.
